## What this is

Before running the model over the full PLOS ONE corpus (about 58,000 articles),
I validate it on a 100-article pilot. Four of us hand-coded those 100 articles
for whether each demographic (gender, race, education, socioeconomic status) is
reported, and the percentage breakdown when it is. That hand coding is the gold
standard. The model reads the same 100 articles, and I score its answers against
ours. If it matches us closely enough, we trust it on the full set. If not, we
fix the extraction first.

The scoring uses three standard measures on each demographic's reported / not
reported flag:

- **Recall**: of the demographics we coded as reported, how many did the model catch.
- **Precision**: of the demographics the model flagged as reported, how many really were.
- **Accuracy**: how often the model got the reported / not call right overall.

## Results

| Demographic | Recall | Precision | Accuracy |
|---|---|---|---|
| Gender | 0.91 | 0.91 | 0.86 |
| Race | 0.86 | 0.83 | 0.93 |
| Education | 0.73 | 0.80 | 0.80 |
| SES | 0.70 | 0.44 | 0.88 |
| **Overall** | **0.84** | **0.82** | **0.87** |

Two supporting numbers: the model split each article into the same number of
participant samples we did in **91%** of cases, and **96 of 100** articles
produced clean, parseable output.

## Reading it

The pattern is consistent. **Recall is strong** on the demographics that get
reported clearly (the model finds what is there), and **precision is the weaker
axis** (it sometimes flags a demographic as reported when the article did not
really report it). Gender, the most commonly reported demographic, meets the bar
on both. Race is close. Education and SES are the soft spots.

Two honest caveats on the soft spots:

- **SES is barely present.** Only 10 of the 100 articles report it, so its
  numbers, precision especially (0.44), swing on four or five individual calls
  and are not stable at that sample size.
- **Education is partly a coding-scheme gap, not model error.** We sometimes
  recorded free-form labels ("undergraduate and graduate") where the model used
  a college / no-college split, and we did not always agree on when education
  counts as reported. Some of the education disagreement is on our side.

## The fix this round

The big improvement was structural. The model had been splitting a single study
into several separate "samples" (one participant pool became two, three, even
six), which misaligned every downstream comparison and was the main thing
dragging precision down. Constraining it to one sample per article, except when
an article truly reports separate participant groups, lifted sample matching
from **0.47 to 0.91** and pulled precision up with it.

## The threshold question

We set a single 0.90 bar on all three measures. On that bar, the pilot does not
pass yet. But that 0.90 was our own choice, set deliberately above what our
source papers actually report (`docs/references.md`: "chosen so we don't cite a
threshold below what these papers already report").

Here is what the literature we cited actually uses, and where we land against it:

| Source | Threshold it uses | Our overall result | Meets it? |
|---|---|---|---|
| Benchmark paper, "study information" tier | recall ≥ 0.80, precision ≥ 0.90 | recall 0.84 | recall yes, precision no |
| Elicit feasibility study | accuracy ≈ 0.87 | accuracy 0.87 | yes |
| GPT second-reviewer paper | precision ≈ 0.91, recall ≈ 0.89 | recall 0.84, precision 0.82 | close, below |

Against the actual literature rather than our rounded-up bar, the model **already
meets the recall tier and the accuracy gate overall**, and **precision (0.82) is
the one axis genuinely below the ~0.90 the papers report**. Gender clears all
three published bars on its own.

Precision is also the most fixable of the three: it is the over-reporting, which
a prompt adjustment (report a demographic only when explicitly stated) and a
tighter SES definition both target directly.

## What I need from the team

Two decisions, and they set what I do next:

1. **Which bar do we hold to?** Our stricter self-imposed 0.90 on every
   demographic, or the tiered thresholds from the papers we actually cite? Under
   the literature framing the model is close to a defensible standard already,
   with precision the remaining gap.

2. **Do we revisit the education and SES coding?** Some of that gap looks like it
   is on our side (the education label mismatch, and SES being too sparse to
   judge at n = 10). Reconciling those would move the numbers legitimately rather
   than by tuning the model.

My plan, pending your call: one more model-side pass (recover the 4 failed
articles, loosen the over-reporting rule to win back recall, add worked examples
to the prompt), then re-score. If education and SES still lag after that, it is a
measurement decision, not more prompt tuning.
